blocks.block_title: Why Documentation Is What Makes a Project a Portfolio Piece
blocks.ava_speaks: ஒரு working architecture, technically impressive-ஆ இருக்கலாம், ஆனா அதை யாருக்கும் explain பண்ண முடியாம இருந்தா, அது ஒரு portfolio piece இல்ல. Real hiring managers-கிட்ட - Freshworks, Zoho, Razorpay மாதிரி companies-ல interview பண்ணும் engineers - ஒரு candidate 'நான் இதை பண்ணேன்'nு சொல்றது போதாது; 'நான் ஏன் இந்த decision எடுத்தேன், என்ன trade-off இருந்துச்சு, எப்படி verify பண்ணேன்'nு சொல்ல முடியணும். FoodQuick-ஓட entire journey - ஒவ்வொரு mistake, ஒவ்வொரு fix - இதுதான் அந்த story-ஐ கொடுக்குது.

rows: 'I designed security groups per tier after seeing how a default-SG mistake exposed a database — here's how I structurally prevented that'
'I set minimum capacity to 2 because I'd seen how min=1 across 2 AZs defeats redundancy during an AZ failure'

blocks.block_title: Your Turn — Write Your Portfolio Narrative
blocks.instruction: இந்த முழு FoodQuick project-ஐ, ஒரு job interview-ல present பண்ண, ஒரு short, structured narrative எழுது.
blocks.scenario: Ravi, இந்த project-ஐ உன் portfolio-ல சேர்க்கும்போது, 'நான் இதை பண்ணேன்' சொல்றதை விட, WHY ஒவ்வொரு decision எடுத்தேன்னு explain பண்ண முடியணும்nு advise பண்ணி இருக்காங்க.

starter_state.current_configuration: No narrative has been written yet

requirements: Describe the architecture in 2-3 sentences (what it is, what it does)
Pick 2 specific decisions (e.g. security-group-per-tier, health check path verification) and explain the mistake each one deliberately avoids
Explain how you verified the deployment beyond a single successful response
End with what you'd do differently or extend next, showing ongoing engineering judgment, not just a finished checklist
hints: Interviewers care more about 'ஏன்' than 'என்ன' - 'நான் security group X create பண்ணேன்' சொல்றதை விட, 'C5.2-ல default security group mistake பார்த்ததால், நான் scoped access design பண்ணேன்'nு சொல்றது ரொம்ப strong
Verification section-ல, C7.3-ஓட student_try exercise (instance termination test) reference பண்ணு - இது 'நான் deep-ஆ verify பண்ணேன்'nு காட்டும்
'What next' section, ஒரு open, honest engineering mindset காட்டும் - example: 'multi-region expansion இன்னும் பண்ணல, அது அடுத்த step'

expected_outcome.verifiable_result: A structured narrative covering the architecture summary, 2 justified decisions tied to specific learned mistakes, the verification approach, and a forward-looking next step
expected_outcome.ava_correct: Correct! இந்த narrative, ஒரு interview-ல confidently present பண்ண முடியற level-ல இருக்கு - decisions-க்கு reasoning இருக்கு, verification depth தெரியுது.
expected_outcome.ava_wrong: Narrative-ஐ ஒரு தடவை படி - 'என்ன பண்ணேன்' மட்டும் சொல்லிட்டு, 'ஏன் அப்படி பண்ணேன்'nு missing-ஆ இருக்கா-ன்னு பாரு. Specific lesson references சேர்த்தா, strong-ஆ இருக்கும்.

blocks.block_title: The Portfolio Project That Couldn't Answer 'Why'
blocks.ava_speaks: priya-dev, ஒரு interview-க்கு prepare பண்றப்போ, தன் FoodQuick project-ஐ present பண்றாங்க - ஆனா interviewer 'ஏன் இந்த security group design தேர்ந்தெடுத்தீங்க?'nு கேட்டப்போ, 'அது தான் standard practice'nு மட்டும் சொன்னாங்க - deeper reasoning இல்லாம.
blocks.setup: priya-dev prepares for a technical interview by memorizing what she built (the architecture components, the AWS services used) but doesn't prepare the reasoning behind specific decisions, assuming 'I built a working 3-tier architecture' would be sufficient.
blocks.what_happened: The interviewer, an experienced cloud architect, asks follow-up 'why' questions — why this security group scoping, why Reserved over Spot for the app tier, why this health check configuration — and priya-dev can only give generic textbook answers, unable to connect decisions back to the specific FoodQuick mistakes that shaped them, even though she genuinely understood and fixed those mistakes during the course.
blocks.broken_config:
Interview preparation: memorized WHAT was built (component list, AWS service names)
Missing: WHY each decision was made, tied to specific reasoning or prior mistakes

Interviewer's actual evaluation criteria: judgment and reasoning depth, not component recall
blocks.error_shown: Interview feedback (paraphrased): 'Candidate clearly built something functional, but couldn't articulate the reasoning behind key architectural decisions — answers felt memorized rather than understood.'
blocks.the_real_problem: priya, உண்மையிலேயே இந்த decisions-ஐ, correct reasons-க்காக தான் எடுத்தாங்க - ஆனா prepare பண்றப்போ, WHAT-ஐ மட்டும் review பண்ணி, WHY-ஐ articulate பண்ண practice பண்ணல. Interview-ல, WHY explain பண்ற ability, WHAT built பண்ணதை விட முக்கியமான signal - ஏன்னா அதுதான் engineering judgment-ஐ காட்டும்.

fix.corrected_config: Before the next interview, priya-dev writes out (like this lesson's student_try exercise) a structured narrative for each major decision, explicitly connecting it back to the specific CS2-CS7 lesson and mistake that shaped it — practicing saying the 'why' out loud, not just knowing it internally.
fix.result: In the next interview, when asked similar 'why' questions, she can clearly trace each decision back to a specific learned lesson, demonstrating exactly the judgment depth interviewers are evaluating for.

blocks.lesson: Understanding WHY a decision was made, ஆனா அதை articulate பண்ண practice பண்ணாம இருக்கறது, இண்டர்வியூ-ல ஒரு real gap-ஆ தெரியும் - internal understanding-ஐ, clear, spoken narrative-ஆ மாத்துறது, ஒரு தனி, deliberate skill.

blocks.block_title: Judgment Round — Reflecting on the Full Journey
blocks.ava_speaks: இப்போ 3 quick scenarios - இந்த முழு course-ஐயும் reflect பண்ணி யோசிச்சு சொல்லு.

challenges.question: Looking back across CS2-CS7, what single pattern showed up most repeatedly across different mistake scenarios (IAM, VPC, S3, EBS, security groups)?
challenges.answer: 'Convenience now, restrict/fix later' — this exact pattern appeared in the IAM offboarding gap, the public-subnet database, the default security group, the disabled Block Public Access, the console-only EBS resize, and the swapped route tables. Recognizing this as a single recurring failure mode, not many unrelated mistakes, is itself a mature engineering insight.

challenges.question: If FoodQuick's team had built this exact 3-tier architecture from day one (instead of the rushed original build), what would have been different about the total effort involved?
challenges.answer: Less total effort overall, even though upfront design takes longer than a quick rushed build — because every retrofit (CS2's investigation, CS3's network redesign, CS5's cost cleanup, etc.) cost significantly more engineering time than getting it right from the start would have. This is the core argument for investing in design before building.

challenges.question: This course's mistake_simulation blocks always show someone ELSE (priya-dev, ananya-analyst, karthik-dev) making the mistake. Why might learning from someone else's realistic mistake be valuable, compared to only learning correct patterns directly?
challenges.answer: Seeing a plausible, realistic path to a mistake — not just 'here's the right way' — builds the pattern recognition needed to catch a similar mistake before making it yourself. Understanding HOW a reasonable person ends up with a public S3 bucket or a swapped route table is more transferable than memorizing the correct configuration alone.

Ravi சொல்றது சரிதான் - இது வெறும் ஒரு course exercise இல்ல, இது தான் நீ real production systems build பண்ண, debug பண்ண, explain பண்ண முடியும்-னு proof. Working Level-ல, இந்த skills-ஐ real incidents-ல apply பண்ணப் போற - அது அடுத்த chapter.
